subjects.title: JavaScript
subjects.description: Core JavaScript language features and runtime behavior

cards.question: What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)?
cards.answer: The window between entering a scope and the point where a `let`/`const` declaration is evaluated. The binding already exists but reading or writing it throws a `ReferenceError`. `var` has no TDZ — it is hoisted and initialized to `undefined`.
hints: It only applies to `let` and `const`, not `var`.

cards.question: What is the difference between `null` and `undefined`?
cards.answer: `undefined` means a variable was declared but never assigned (the default absence). `null` is an intentional "no value" you assign yourself. `typeof undefined` is `"undefined"`, but `typeof null` is `"object"`. `null == undefined` is `true`; `null === undefined` is `false`.

cards.question: What is the difference between `slice` and `splice` on arrays?
cards.answer: `slice(start, end)` returns a shallow copy of a portion and **does not** mutate the array. `splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` **mutates** the array in place (removing and/or inserting) and returns the removed elements.
hints: One of them mutates the original.

cards.question: What does `Array.prototype.reduce` do?
cards.answer:
It folds an array into a single value by running a reducer `(acc, cur) => ...` left to right, threading an accumulator.

```javascript
[1, 2, 3, 4].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); // 10
```
With no initial value the first element seeds the accumulator (and an empty array throws).

cards.question: What is the difference between `map` and `forEach`?
cards.answer: `map` returns a **new array** of the callback's return values (a transform). `forEach` returns `undefined` and exists only for side effects. Neither mutates the source array unless your callback does.

cards.question: What is event delegation?
cards.answer: Attaching one listener to a common ancestor and using event **bubbling** plus `event.target` to handle events from many descendants. Benefits: fewer listeners and it automatically covers elements added later.

cards.question: What is the event loop?
cards.answer: The mechanism that lets single-threaded JS handle async work. The call stack runs synchronous code; when it empties, the loop pulls queued callbacks. The whole **microtask** queue (Promises) drains before the next **macrotask** (timers, I/O).

cards.question: What is the difference between a microtask and a macrotask?
cards.answer: **Microtasks** (Promise reactions, `queueMicrotask`, `MutationObserver`) run right after the current task and the entire microtask queue drains before anything else. **Macrotasks** (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`, I/O, UI events) run one per event-loop turn. So a resolved Promise's `.then` runs before a `setTimeout(…, 0)`.

cards.question: How does `Promise.all` differ from `Promise.allSettled`?
cards.answer: `Promise.all` is **fail-fast**: it rejects as soon as any input rejects, otherwise resolves to an array of values. `Promise.allSettled` **never rejects**: it waits for every input and resolves to `{ status, value | reason }` objects, so you can inspect each outcome.

cards.question: What is a generator function?
What is the prototype chain?
cards.answer: Every object has an internal `[[Prototype]]` link. A property lookup walks up the chain until the key is found or the chain ends at `null`. This is how inheritance works in JS. Read the link with `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`; it usually ends at `Object.prototype` then `null`.

cards.question: What does `Object.freeze` do?
cards.answer: Makes an object immutable: you can't add, remove, or reassign its properties (silently ignored in sloppy mode, throws in strict mode). It is **shallow** — nested objects stay mutable unless you freeze them too.

cards.question: What is destructuring assignment?
What is the difference between `for...in` and `for...of`?
cards.answer: `for...in` iterates enumerable **keys**, including inherited ones — meant for objects, but use with care. `for...of` iterates **values** of any iterable (arrays, strings, `Map`, `Set`). For arrays, prefer `for...of`.

cards.question: What is the difference between spread and rest?
cards.answer: Same `...` token, opposite jobs. **Spread** expands an iterable or object into individual elements/props (in calls and literals). **Rest** collects the remaining items into an array/object (in parameters and destructuring).

cards.question: What is currying?
cards.answer: Transforming a function of N arguments into N nested unary functions, each returning the next: `f(a)(b)(c)`. It enables partial application and easy composition.

cards.question: What is memoization?
cards.answer: Caching a function's results keyed by its arguments so repeated calls with the same inputs return the cached value instead of recomputing. It trades memory for speed and only works for **pure** functions.

cards.question: What is the difference between `call`, `apply`, and `bind`?
cards.answer: All three set `this`. `call(thisArg, ...args)` invokes immediately with args listed individually. `apply(thisArg, argsArray)` invokes immediately with args as an array. `bind(thisArg, ...args)` returns a **new** function with `this` (and any preset args) permanently bound, without calling it.

cards.question: What is a Promise and what states can it be in?
cards.answer: An object representing a value that may be available later. States: **pending** → either **fulfilled** (with a value) or **rejected** (with a reason). Settling is one-way and final. You react with `.then` / `.catch` / `.finally`.

cards.question: What do `async` and `await` do?
cards.answer: `async` makes a function always return a Promise. `await` pauses the function until a Promise settles, yielding its value (or throwing its rejection), letting you write async code in a synchronous style. Handle errors with `try/catch`.

cards.question: What is optional chaining (`?.`)?
cards.answer: It short-circuits and returns `undefined` when a reference is `null` or `undefined`, instead of throwing. Works for property access, indexing, and calls: `a?.b`, `a?.[i]`, `fn?.()`.

cards.question: What is the nullish coalescing operator (`??`)?
cards.answer:
It returns the right operand only when the left is `null` or `undefined` — not for other falsy values like `0` or `''`. Contrast with `||`, which falls back on **any** falsy value.

```javascript
0 ?? 5;  // 0
0 || 5;  // 5
```

cards.question: What are template literals?
cards.answer: Backtick strings that support multi-line text and `${expression}` interpolation. They also enable **tagged templates**, where a function receives the string parts and the interpolated values separately.

cards.question: What is the difference between a shallow and a deep copy?
cards.answer: A **shallow** copy duplicates only the top level and shares nested references (`{...obj}`, `Object.assign`, `arr.slice()`). A **deep** copy recursively clones everything (`structuredClone`, or `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` with caveats).

cards.question: What is `structuredClone`?
cards.answer: A built-in that **deep-clones** most values — objects, arrays, `Map`, `Set`, `Date`, typed arrays, and even cyclic references. It cannot clone functions, DOM nodes, or prototype chains (those throw or are dropped).

cards.question: What is the difference between a function declaration and a function expression?
cards.answer: A **declaration** (`function f() {}`) is fully hoisted, so it's callable before its line. An **expression** (`const f = function () {}`) is not — only the variable binding hoists per `var`/`let` rules. Arrow functions are always expressions.

cards.question: What are the falsy values in JavaScript?
cards.answer: Exactly eight: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `''` (empty string), `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN`. Everything else is truthy — including `'0'`, `'false'`, `[]`, and `{}`.

cards.question: How do a `Map` and a plain object differ?
cards.answer: A `Map` allows **any** key type (objects, functions), preserves insertion order, exposes `size`, and is directly iterable. A plain object coerces keys to strings/symbols, carries a prototype, and needs `Object.keys`/`entries`. Maps are better for frequently added/removed dynamic keys.

cards.question: What is a `Set`?
cards.answer: A collection of **unique** values (compared with SameValueZero). It has fast `add`/`has`/`delete`, a `size`, and iterates in insertion order. Common trick: dedupe an array with `[...new Set(arr)]`.

cards.question: What do `Object.keys`, `Object.values`, and `Object.entries` return?
cards.answer: All three return arrays over an object's **own enumerable string-keyed** properties: `keys` → the keys, `values` → the values, `entries` → `[key, value]` pairs (handy with `for...of` and `Object.fromEntries`).

cards.question: What is short-circuit evaluation?
cards.answer: `&&` returns the first **falsy** operand (or the last operand if all are truthy); `||` returns the first **truthy** operand (or the last if all are falsy). Evaluation stops once the result is determined — used for guards and defaults.

cards.question: What is the difference between `throw`ing an error and returning one?
cards.answer: `throw` unwinds the call stack until a `try/catch` handles it (or the program crashes), interrupting control flow. Returning an error value keeps normal control flow and forces the caller to check the result. Both are valid; pick per API style.

cards.question: What does the `new` operator do?
cards.answer: Four steps: (1) create a fresh object, (2) link its `[[Prototype]]` to the constructor's `.prototype`, (3) bind `this` to it and run the constructor body, (4) return that object — unless the constructor explicitly returns its own object.

cards.question: What is a `Symbol` used for?
cards.answer: A primitive that produces **unique**, collision-free identifiers. Common uses: non-enumerable object keys and well-known protocols like `Symbol.iterator` (which makes a value iterable) and `Symbol.asyncIterator`.

cards.question: What is the difference between `Object.create(null)` and `{}`?
cards.answer: `{}` inherits from `Object.prototype`, so it has `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, etc. `Object.create(null)` has **no prototype** — a bare dictionary with no inherited keys, immune to prototype-pollution and key collisions like a `"toString"` key.

cards.question: What does `typeof NaN` return?
cards.answer: `NaN` ("Not a Number") is itself a value of the number type, so `typeof NaN` is `"number"`.

cards.question: What does `[1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2)` return?
cards.answer: `map` returns a new array of each callback result.

cards.question: What does `'5' + 3` evaluate to?
cards.answer: With a string operand, `+` concatenates: the number `3` is coerced to `"3"`, giving `"53"`.

cards.question: What does `'5' - 3` evaluate to?
cards.answer: `-` has no string meaning, so `'5'` is coerced to the number `5`, giving `2`.

cards.question: What does `typeof function () {}` return?
cards.answer: Functions are callable objects, but `typeof` reports them specially as `"function"`.

cards.question: What does `[1, 2, 3].indexOf(4)` return?
cards.answer: `indexOf` returns `-1` when the value is not found.

cards.question: What does `Boolean('')` return?
cards.answer: An empty string is one of the eight falsy values.

cards.question: What does `Boolean('0')` return?
cards.answer: Any non-empty string is truthy — including `'0'`, `'false'`, and `' '`.

cards.question: What does `[10, 9, 1].sort()` return?
cards.answer: The default `sort` converts elements to strings and compares lexicographically: `"1" < "10" < "9"`. Use `sort((a, b) => a - b)` for numbers.

cards.question: What does `Promise.resolve(1).then(x => x + 1)` resolve to?
cards.answer: `.then` returns a new Promise resolved with the callback's return value, `2`.
Synchronous code runs first (`A`, `D`). Then the microtask (`C`) drains before the `setTimeout` macrotask (`B`).

cards.question: What does `[1, 2, 3, 4].filter(n => n % 2 === 0)` return?
cards.answer: `filter` keeps the elements for which the callback is truthy — the even numbers.

cards.question: What does `0 == ''` evaluate to?
cards.answer: Loose equality coerces both sides to numbers: `''` becomes `0`, so `0 == 0` is `true`. `0 === ''` would be `false`.

cards.question: What does `NaN === NaN` evaluate to?
cards.answer: `NaN` is never equal to anything, including itself. Detect it with `Number.isNaN`.

cards.question: What does `parseInt('08px', 10)` return?
cards.answer: `parseInt` reads leading characters that form a valid integer and stops at the first invalid one, giving `8`.

cards.question: What does `[...'abc']` produce?
cards.answer: Strings are iterable, so spreading yields an array of characters.

cards.question: What does `JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: 1 })` return?
cards.answer: `JSON.stringify` omits properties whose value is `undefined` (and functions).

cards.question: What does `typeof []` return?
cards.answer: Arrays are objects, so `typeof []` is `"object"`. Use `Array.isArray` to detect arrays.

cards.question: What does `1 < 2 < 3` evaluate to?
cards.answer: It evaluates left to right: `(1 < 2)` is `true`, then `true < 3` coerces `true` to `1`, and `1 < 3` is `true`. (Beware: `3 < 2 < 1` is also `true`.)

cards.question: What does `[10, 1, 2].sort((a, b) => a - b)` return?
cards.answer: A numeric comparator sorts ascending by value.

cards.question: What does `typeof arguments` return inside a normal function?
cards.answer: `arguments` is an array-like object, so `typeof` is `"object"`. (It does not exist in arrow functions.)

cards.question: Given `const { a = 5 } = { a: undefined }`, what is `a`?
cards.answer: A destructuring default applies when the property value is `undefined`, so `a` is `5`.

cards.question: What does `[1, [2, [3]]].flat()` return?
cards.answer: `flat()` flattens one level by default, leaving the deeper `[3]` nested. Use `flat(Infinity)` to fully flatten.

cards.question: Which array method returns the **first** element that satisfies a test function?
cards.answer: `find` returns the first matching element, or `undefined` if none match.

cards.question: Which array method returns `true` if **at least one** element passes the test function?
cards.answer: `some` returns `true` as soon as any element passes.

cards.question: Which array method joins all elements into a single string with an optional separator?
cards.answer: `join` concatenates the elements, e.g. `[1,2,3].join('-')` → `"1-2-3"`.

cards.question: Which array method adds one or more elements to the **end** and returns the new length?
cards.answer: `push` appends to the end and mutates the array.

cards.question: Which array method removes and returns the **last** element?
cards.answer: `pop` removes the last element (mutating the array).

cards.question: Which array method removes and returns the **first** element?
cards.answer: `shift` removes the first element and shifts the rest down.

cards.question: Which array method adds one or more elements to the **beginning** of an array?
cards.answer: `unshift` prepends elements and returns the new length.

cards.question: Which string method returns a section between two indexes, supports negatives, and does not mutate?
cards.answer: `slice(start, end)` extracts a substring; negative indexes count from the end.

cards.question: Which array method flattens nested sub-arrays one level deep by default?
cards.answer: `flat()` returns a new array with sub-array elements concatenated one level deep.

cards.question: Which global function schedules a callback to run once after a delay in milliseconds?
cards.answer: `setTimeout(fn, ms)` queues the callback as a macrotask.

cards.question: Which `Promise` combinator settles as soon as the **first** input promise settles?
cards.answer: `Promise.race` adopts the first settled outcome (fulfilled or rejected).

cards.question: Which `Promise` combinator waits for **all** inputs and never rejects?
cards.answer: `Promise.allSettled` resolves to an array of `{ status, value | reason }`.

cards.question: Which method copies enumerable own properties from source objects onto a target object?
cards.answer: `Object.assign(target, ...sources)` performs a shallow merge and returns the target.

cards.question: Which array method tests whether a value is present, returning a boolean?
cards.answer: `includes` returns `true`/`false` (and matches `NaN`, unlike `indexOf`).

cards.question: Which static method creates a new array from an iterable or array-like value?
cards.answer: `Array.from(iterable)` builds a real array (optionally with a map function).

cards.question: Which method returns `true` if a property exists **directly** on an object (not inherited)?
cards.answer: `hasOwnProperty` checks own properties only (`obj.hasOwnProperty('x')`).

cards.question: Which built-in deep-clones most values, including cyclic references?
cards.answer: `structuredClone(value)` produces a deep copy (no functions or DOM nodes).

cards.question: Which array method returns the index of the first element matching a test function?
cards.answer: `findIndex` returns the index, or `-1` if no element matches.

cards.question: Match each `typeof` expression to its result.
cards.answer: `typeof` returns a lowercase string naming the operand's type.

cards.question: Match each array method to whether it mutates the original array.
cards.answer: Mutating methods change the array in place; the others return a new array.

cards.question: Match each JavaScript expression to its value.
cards.answer: Only the eight falsy values coerce to `false`; everything else is truthy.
